questions.title: File I/O practice 1
questions.prompt: Which type represents a file-system path?
choices: Path
FileText
Scanner
StringBuilder
questions.explanation: `Path` represents a location and can be passed to Files operations. A String contains characters but does not provide the file-system abstraction.

questions.title: File I/O practice 2
choices: It closes the stream automatically
It sorts every line
It prevents IOException at compile time
It converts the file to an array
questions.explanation: The stream holds an open file resource. Try-with-resources calls its close method even when processing throws an exception.

questions.title: Trace File I/O
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The same Path is used for writing and reading. UTF-8 makes the text encoding an explicit part of the file format. The resulting output is 'CS101\nMATH120'.

questions.title: File I/O practice 5
questions.prompt: What do the CREATE and APPEND options change about `Files.writeString`?
choices: New text is added to the end of the file instead of replacing what is there
The file is deleted first, then rewritten
The write is retried automatically if it fails
The text is compressed before writing
questions.explanation: By default `writeString` truncates: it replaces the whole file. `APPEND` makes it add to the end, and `CREATE` makes the file first if it does not exist. Without APPEND the earlier contents are lost. The options do not delete, retry, or compress.

questions.title: Replacing records
questions.prompt: Before writing student records to an existing file, what should the program decide?
choices: Decide whether to replace, append, or rewrite updated data before opening the file.
Overwrite existing records when the task calls for appending.
Assume every file path starts in the source-code folder.
Read data before checking for an I/O failure.
questions.explanation: A write can succeed and still destroy needed data if the code meant to append or update carefully. File code should make the replacement-versus-append decision explicit before it touches the existing file.

questions.title: Path objects
questions.prompt: Why use `Path` for file locations instead of hand-built strings?
choices: Ignore character encoding for shared text files.
Represent locations with Path.
Leave closeable resources unmanaged.
Catch an IOException where no useful response is possible.
questions.explanation: `Path` represents a filesystem location without forcing the program to stitch separators by hand. That makes code easier to read and less fragile across operating systems and project layouts.

questions.title: Portable text encoding
questions.prompt: A Java program writes names that may be opened on different computers. What should it specify?
choices: Use one giant string for a large file.
Build paths with fragile string concatenation.
Select UTF-8 for portable text.
Treat a missing file as an empty valid file every time.
questions.explanation: Choosing UTF-8 makes text encoding predictable instead of depending on a machine default. That matters most when files move between computers or include characters outside plain ASCII.

questions.title: Append or replace
questions.prompt: A report should add today's line without erasing yesterday's lines. What decision matters most?
choices: Write output before validating the destination.
Ignore partial read or parse failures.
Use platform-specific separators in portable code.
Decide whether a write replaces or appends.
questions.explanation: The write mode must match the job. Appending preserves earlier content and adds to it; replacement rewrites the file. Naming that choice in code prevents quiet data loss.

questions.title: Handling IOException
questions.prompt: Where should a Java program handle an `IOException`?
choices: Handle IOException at a layer that can respond.
Hide the original file error behind a vague message.
Read all lines when streaming would keep memory smaller.
Assume the default charset is always the intended one.
questions.explanation: Handle an I/O failure where the code can do something useful, such as retry, choose another path, or show a clear message. Catching it too low often hides context; ignoring it leaves callers guessing.

questions.title: Streaming large files
questions.prompt: How should code read a large file without loading the whole thing into memory?
choices: Mix persistence code with unrelated calculations.
Stream large files and close the stream automatically.
Open the same file twice for conflicting operations.
Forget that write modes can replace existing data.
questions.explanation: Streaming processes one piece at a time and pairs well with try-with-resources or APIs that close automatically. It keeps memory use steady and still lets the program count, filter, or transform lines.
